title: How far does the spinning Earth push?
hook: The Earth turns under anything that moves. Over a long trip, how big is the drift?

doesNotKnow: how small or large the Coriolis drift is for ordinary motion
that the drift grows with the square of the travel time

misconception: The Coriolis effect is what makes a sink drain one way, and it is large for anything that moves.
objective: The learner can explain that, seen from the turning ground, an unsteered object drifts sideways by an amount that grows with the square of the travel time: tens of metres over 10 km, hundreds of km over 1,000 km at 45°N, and zero at the equator.

claims.text: On a frictionless platform spinning like the Earth at 45°N, an object sliding north at 100 m/s for 1,000 km ends up about 470 km east of its aim.
claims.source: Toy model (f-plane, labelled on the stage): f = 2 Ω sin φ, Ω = 7.2921e-5 rad/s (IERS value; from memory). Exact inertial-circle solution x = (v/f)(1 - cos ft), y = (v/f) sin ft with path length v t = 1,000 km: x = 471.5 km, y = 831.9 km (drift() in Demo.tsx; node check). Changed from the brief's small-deflection formula Ω sin φ v t² (515.6 km), which is not valid when ft ≈ 1 (here 1.03 rad). Both round to 'about 500 km'. On the real rotating sphere latitude changes by about 7.5° over the run; the toy holds it fixed. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Re-derived in node: f = 2*7.2921e-5*sin45 = 1.0313e-4 /s; 1,000 km at 100 m/s = 1e4 s, ft = 1.031 rad, east = (v/f)(1-cos ft) = 471.5 km (stage shows ~470). Toy is labelled on the stage; the small-angle formula would give 515.6 km, which the lesson does not use.

claims.text: Over 10 km the same object drifts about 52 m, and over 100 km about 5.2 km.
claims.source: Same toy: 0.0516 km and 5.152 km at 45°N, 100 m/s (drift()). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: 10 km -> 0.0516 km (52 m); 100 km -> 5.152 km (5.2 km) at 45N.

claims.text: The drift grows with the square of the travel time; 100 times the distance gave about 9,000 times the drift, a bit under 100² because the long path curls.
claims.source: For small ft, x ≈ (1/2) f v t² = Ω sin φ v t². Ratio 471.5 / 0.0516 = 9,138 (rounded to 9,000 in the reveal), versus 10,000 for a pure square law. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: 471.5 / 0.0516 = 9,145, shown as 'about 9,000'; pure square law would give 10,000; small-angle x ~ (1/2) f v t^2 so drift scales with t^2 for short runs.

claims.text: The Coriolis effect is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles.
claims.source: The horizontal deflection is set by f = 2 Ω sin φ: 0 at φ = 0, maximum at φ = 90°. The stage's latitude slider shows 0 m at 0°N. Holton, An Introduction to Dynamic Meteorology (from memory). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): f = 2 Omega sin(lat) is 0 at the equator and largest at the poles (Holton, Intro to Dynamic Meteorology, ch. 1/2). Node: latitude 0 gives 0 m east; slider shows it.

claims.text: The Coriolis effect shapes winds and ocean currents over hundreds of kilometres.
claims.source: Large-scale winds and currents are close to geostrophic balance, in which the Coriolis term balances the pressure gradient (Holton, ch. 3; from memory, not checked online). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Large-scale winds and ocean currents are close to geostrophic balance (Coriolis vs pressure gradient), a standard result (Holton ch. 3; Vallis, Atmospheric and Oceanic Fluid Dynamics). 'Hundreds of kilometres' is the usual synoptic-scale threshold.

recall.question: Why does the Coriolis effect matter for a storm system but not for a ball you throw across a garden?
options: Storms are made of air, balls are solid
The drift grows with the square of the travel time, so it is tiny for short trips
The Coriolis effect only works over water
recall.why: Drift grows roughly with time squared: 100 times the distance gives roughly 10,000 times the drift, so it is negligible over metres and huge over hundreds of kilometres.
